title: Tony Mazzocchi Embodied the Best of the Labor Movement
summary: In the latter half of the 20th century, labor leader Tony Mazzocchi fought for a progressive political vision that put working-class concerns front and center. His example continues to be invaluable for labor and the Left today.
reason: This is primarily a representational/hagiographic piece about a historical figure rather than a story that illuminates a capture mechanism, routing architecture, or commune layer in operation.

title: For Iranians, Despair Is Not Strategy

title: The Donroe Doctrine: Making LatAm an Investor’s Paradise
summary: The Trump administration is forcing Latin American governments into arbitration courts that grant multinationals the extraordinary power to sue states that nationalize resources or even just raise the minimum wage, if perceived to threaten investor profits.
reason: This story shows enclosure operating at a structural level — investor arbitration courts are a routing architecture that redirects sovereign decision-making power away from states and populations toward capital, making democratic resource control illegible.
angle: Use the routing architecture tool: arbitration courts don't just protect investors, they reroute the flow of political power so that democratic decisions (minimum wage, nationalization) become liabilities, structurally encoding capital's veto into governance.

title: We Are Watching the Rise of Democratic Fascism
summary: Bertolt Brecht predicted it in 1942: American fascism would be democratic in the American fashion. He was right. That's precisely what makes it so hard to stop.
reason: This is a representational-register argument about labeling and framing current politics, not an analysis of a concrete capture mechanism in operation.

title: Donald Trump Is on a Mining Offensive in DR Congo
summary: The Trump administration wants a new sphere of influence in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. US businesses are already rushing in, but many locals insist their mineral wealth should be for the Congolese themselves.
reason: This story directly illustrates enclosure of a common substrate (mineral wealth embedded in social and ecological commons) by a state-corporate alliance, with local resistance articulating an explicit counter-claim to commons ownership.
angle: Use the routing architecture tool to show how US-backed mining deals route resource flows away from Congolese communities and through transnational capital circuits, while locals asserting 'mineral wealth for the Congolese' represent an attempt to re-route those flows through a different productive circuit.

title: The Corporate Thriller Lied to Us
summary: Criterion Channel is hosting a retrospective on Hollywood’s “corporate thrillers” from the 1980s through the early 2000s. If anything, their message about the capitalist rot in America’s institutions looks far too tame for how the last couple of decades turned out.
reason: This is primarily representational critique — new framing of old content — with no routing-level change or commune layer activity to analyze.

title: Capitalism Was Built on the Ruins of the Commons
summary: The Industrial Revolution's chief product was not goods, but a new class of laborers who owned nothing and worked to survive. Historian Peter Linebaugh traces the creation of this working class through the violent enclosure of the commons they once relied on.
reason: Directly theorizes the founding enclosure of the commons and the production of the proletariat as a class — the historical substrate of the entire framework.
angle: Use the enclosure thesis as the origin story of the capture sequence: not metaphor but historical mechanism, showing how the common was materially destroyed to produce wage dependency.

title: Messing With Childcare Ratios Is a Terrible Idea
summary: Donald Trump’s childcare czar says he wants federal regulations for daycare centers to “fit on an index card in my back pocket.” His plans contain many causes for alarm, not least his dangerous proposal to raise child-to-adult ratios.
reason: Childcare deregulation is a direct attack on the commune layer — the reproductive labor infrastructure that capital depends on but refuses to adequately fund — and exposes the alibi that deregulation serves families.
angle: Use the 'reproductive labor as commons' lens: childcare is a substrate the market extracts from but cannot produce on its own terms, and raising ratios is enclosure by degradation — making the common less viable to force dependence on market substitutes or unpaid domestic labor.

title: This Doomsday Law Could Stop Trains Across America In A Matter of Weeks
summary: Arbitrary insurance requirements set by Congress could easily kill commuter rail in the United States.
reason: Insurance mandates function as a routing architecture that channels public transit funds toward liability markets while making collective infrastructure illegible as a public good.
angle: Use the routing architecture tool to show how the insurance requirement doesn't just regulate rail but structurally redirects resources away from the commune layer of shared transit infrastructure toward private risk markets.

title: Lasers, hawks and even guns haven’t solved the UK’s pigeon problem. There is a better way | Sydney Lobe
summary: Councils spend heavily on grisly yet ineffective methods. Why won’t they consider a proven, low-cost and humane strategy? By some estimates there are almost 3 million pigeons residing in London, which has the highest pigeon population in the country. Known as “rats with wings”, “flying ashtrays” and “gutter birds”, pigeons do not have popular sentiment on their side. And cities in the UK have an extensive history of attempted pigeon pest control – having tried everything short of an exorcism to remove them – to no avail. London’s best-known victory in the war against pigeons was self-declared, after an operation in Trafalgar Square in the early 2000s .
